links.note: In 1247 the pope sent two men to revise the Carmelite rule. They were Hugh, a cardinal, and William, bishop of Tortosa. The editor of Teresa's Foundations says both were Dominicans. Their letter calls the Carmelites friars, while the pope's own letter still calls them hermits. Neither letter says that the Dominicans shaped the order. So this tie is thin.

sources.work: Hugh of Saint-Cher and William of Tortosa, letter to the Carmelites with the revised Rule (1247), in Innocent IV's confirmation, trans. Lewis (1913)

sources.work: Innocent IV, letter of confirmation of the revised Carmelite Rule (1247), salutation, trans. Lewis (1913)
sources.quote: Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to His beloved children the prior and brethren, hermits of blessed Mary of Mount Carmel, health and the apostolic blessing.

sources.work: Benedict Zimmerman, note to the Rule, in The Book of the Foundations (1913)

links.note: At the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, the Greek side made a profession of faith. In it they accepted the full primacy of the Roman church. Its 1911 editor says Pope Clement IV first put the text to Emperor Michael VIII in 1267. Michael then offered it to Pope Gregory X at Lyon. The profession does not show how the Greek church received the union.

sources.work: Profession of faith of Michael VIII Palaiologos (1274), in Denzinger, Enchiridion symbolorum, ed. Bannwart (1911), on the Roman primacy
sources.quote: quem se ab ipso Domino in beato PETRO Apostolorum principe sive vertice, cuius Romanus Pontifex est successor, cum potestatis plenitudine recepisse veraciter et humiliter recognoscit.

sources.work: First Vatican Council, Pastor aeternus, ch. 4 (1870), on the Greeks' profession at Lyon, in Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 2 (1878), English
sources.quote: with the approval of the Second Council of Lyons, the Greeks professed that the holy Roman Church enjoys su- preme and full primacy and pre- eminence over the whole Catholic Church,

sources.work: Clemens Bannwart (ed.), Denzinger, Enchiridion symbolorum, 11th ed. (1911), heading and note to nos. 461-466 (the profession of Michael VIII)

links.note: William of Tyre was archbishop of Tyre in the crusader kingdom. He wrote that the Maronites joined the Latin church around 1182. This rests on modern historians of the Maronites, not on his own text.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse University Press, 1986; repr. Gorgias 2005)

links.note: The monks of Cîteaux set out to keep the Rule of St Benedict more plainly. No early Cistercian text quoted here says so in their own words. A 1907 editor of the Rule notes only that early Cistercian statutes, like the Rule, set times when monks might talk.

sources.work: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, note on the Rule's provisions for silence, in The Rule of St. Benedict (1907)

links.note: The Philokalia calls Nicetas Stethatos a priest of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, the house of Theodore the Studite. It makes him the closest pupil of Symeon the New Theologian, around 1030. That ties Stoudios to Symeon's circle. But no source quoted here shows the monks of Athos drawing on the monks who fought for icons.

sources.work: Philokalia ton hieron neptikon, vol. 2 (Athens, 1893), preface to Nicetas Stethatos

links.note: Bernard of Clairvaux, the Cistercians' best-known abbot, wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood in defense of the Templars. He argued that a knight who killed in this cause was killing evil, not a man. This rests on the modern history of the order, not on Bernard's own text.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber, The New Knighthood: A History of the Order of the Temple (Cambridge University Press, 1994)

links.note: In 1215 the Maronite patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti went to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council. A papal bull then set out the terms of the union. This rests on modern historians of the Maronites, not on the bull or the council's acts.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse University Press, 1986; repr. Gorgias 2005)

links.note: Theodosius, abbot of the Caves Monastery at Kyiv, gave his monks the rule of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople. A Russian church history of 1838 says a monk who came with the new metropolitan, George, brought the rule from that city. The Kyiv texts it draws on are not quoted here.

sources.work: A. N. Mouravieff, A History of the Church of Russia (1838; trans. R. W. Blackmore, Oxford, 1842)

links.note: The Caves Monastery at Kyiv spans the year 1054. A Russian church history of 1838 says that the priest Hilarion, later the city's chief bishop, first prayed in a cave there. The hermit Anthony then settled in Hilarion's empty cave, and Theodosius later gave the growing community its rule. It draws on a Kyivan chronicle not quoted here.

sources.work: A. N. Mouravieff, A History of the Church of Russia (1838; trans. R. W. Blackmore, Oxford, 1842)

links.note: In 1440 Pope Eugenius IV wrote of a hermitage in Spain where Franciscan friars lived. He said they lived under the observance of the Rule of blessed Francis. In 1438 he had confirmed Bernardino of Siena as head of the order's Observant houses in Italy. That letter says the houses were set up 'under the holy name of observance'.

sources.work: Eugenius IV, letter to the abbot of Santa María de Carracedo, Florence, 28 August 1440, on the hermitage at Caboca de Alva, in Bullarium Franciscanum, Nova Series I, ed. Huntemann (1929), no. 485
sources.quote: in quo plures ex fratribus Minoribus sub observan- tia regulae beati Francisci degunt pro praesenti,

sources.work: Eugenius IV, Ad futuram rei memoriam, Ferrara, 1 September 1438, confirming William of Casale's letter that made Bernardino of Siena vicar of the Observant houses, in Bullarium Franciscanum, Nova Series I, ed. Huntemann (1929), no. 385
